Done. Here's the report.

## The idea, in one sentence

An open pop-up book in perspective — the minute is a card cut to the numeral and creased **down its middle, between the two digits**, so each digit sits whole on its own panel of a V-fold standing in a slot in the right page; the hour is a **flat die-cut card leaning out of the left page**; the seconds are a **pull tab** creeping out of a slot; and on the hour the right page lifts off the spread, stands edge-on and lies down on the left, **turning the spread over**.

Pitched and rejected: a letterpress/composing-stick clock (the printed sheet is a static picture — the clock reading is indirect) and a folded-inkblot clock (mirrored numerals don't read). `origami` already owns flat-sheet folding, so the pop-up's own mechanisms — die-cut, V-fold, slot, pull tab, page turn — are what the time is made of.

## Renders (all in `.claude/skills/oled-clock/out/`)

| file | what |
|---|---|
| `popup-ds.png` | the still, 10:09 |
| `popup-ds-digits.png` | the ten numerals, each in the minute slot |
| `popup-ds-turn.png` | minute turn, 10:09:58 + 3.2 s (sinks, beat, new one pushes up) |
| `popup-ds-hour.png` | hour turn, 10:59:58 + 3.2 s (the leaf turns) |
| `popup-ds.gif`, `popup-ds-hour.gif` | 300 frames, 50 fps |
| `popup-ds-wear.png` | burn-in map |

## check.mjs

```
popup-ds (Pop-up, 096-128x64, 60 fps on SPI 10 MHz)
  worst frame : 0.83 ms, 1024 RAM bytes  -> bus allows 1211 fps   frames over budget: 0
  pixels lit, on average : 25.7% of the glass
  hottest pixel : 21.0 h/day, 16.4 h/day full-contrast equivalent (~1.7 years to 50%)
  PASS
```
Wear is in line with the shipped faces (`flip` 21.4 h / 1.6 y, `numberfolk` 23.5 h / 2.0 y). It needed a fix: the dithers were anchored to the glass, so a lit page pixel stayed lit *all day*; they now walk with the orbit (`dither(px-OX, py-OY, …)`).

`frame()` is pure (every still, sheet and GIF frame is a single call at an arbitrary time) and costs 0.83 ms of the 16.7 ms frame.

## The honest weakest point

**The letterform is ordinary and the paper read is carried by too little.** Each numeral really is a folded card — cut counters, crease, two panels at different angles, cast shadow, slot, and a fold that opens and closes in the transition — but at 5–6 px stroke weight the fold can only be stated as a *tonal* difference between two big panels, and the digits themselves are a plain seven-segment figure. So at arm's length a stranger reads "two chunky numerals on a dark plane" before reading "folded paper": the mechanism is in the motion, not in the still. What I'd fix next: draw a letterform whose strokes are cut on a diagonal (a hand-cut look) so the silhouette itself, not the shading, says paper — and fold the card on a line that runs between strokes rather than across the digital waist. The book is also mostly inferred in a still — from the gutter, the perspective and the two page-block bands — rather than seen.
